opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think we're at a really exciting inflection point. Language models have shown what happens when you train at scale on internet data, but physics is fundamentally different. The world isn't made of tokens. It's made of continuous phenomena: fluid flows, electromagnetic fields, molecular interactions, weather systems. So the big question for me has always been, how do we build foundation models that actually understand physical reality rather than just pattern-matching on text about it?

That's a big part of why we developed neural operators. The key idea is that instead of learning mappings between finite-dimensional vectors, you learn mappings between function spaces. That gives you resolution invariance: you can train on coarse data and evaluate at much finer resolutions, which matters enormously in scientific domains, where data comes from many sources at very different fidelities. You might have cheap low-resolution simulations, expensive high-fidelity ones, and sparse experimental measurements, and you want one model that can absorb all of it.

When I think about foundation models for physics, I see a few key ingredients. First, the architecture has to respect the structure of the problem: continuity, symmetries, conservation laws. Second, you need to combine data with physics knowledge. We've done a lot of work on physics-informed neural operators, where you add PDE constraints into the loss so the model doesn't just fit the data but stays consistent with known physics. That helps you generalize, especially where data is scarce. Third, you want models that transfer across problems, so pretraining on a broad family of PDEs and fine-tuning for specific applications.

We've already seen what's possible. FourCastNet showed that AI weather models could match traditional numerical weather prediction at tens of thousands of times the speed. Since then the whole field of AI weather forecasting has exploded. That's a proof point that these models aren't just academic curiosities. They can be operationally useful.

Where I see this going is toward models that can do science, not just accelerate simulation. Imagine designing a new aircraft wing, a better battery, a fusion reactor component, or a medical device, with an AI that can rapidly explore the design space, run what are effectively millions of simulations in seconds, and propose candidates that actually work in the physical world. We've done things like designing medical catheters that reduce bacterial contamination, where the neural operator explored geometries far faster than traditional solvers could.

The other piece I'm passionate about is that language models alone won't get us there. LLMs can help with reasoning, literature, and hypothesis generation, but they hallucinate, and in science and engineering hallucinations can be dangerous. You need grounding in physical reality. So I see the future as a combination: language models for high-level reasoning and interfacing with humans, tightly coupled with physics-grounded models like neural operators that can actually simulate and verify. That's how we get to AI that accelerates scientific discovery in a trustworthy way.

r001.rationale: The response proposes models pretrained across broad families of PDEs and describes applications spanning fluid flows, electromagnetic fields, molecules, weather, and engineering design.

r002.rationale: It names several physical phenomena and discusses physical constraints, but does not say the models capture coupling among different physical processes.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, it's great to be here.

So I think the future of foundation models for physics is really about moving from learning in the space of data to learning in the space of functions. Most of what we call AI today operates on discrete tokens or pixels. But the physical world is continuous. Fluid flow, weather, the stresses in a material, the electromagnetic fields in a chip — these are functions defined over space and time, governed by partial differential equations. So the question we've been asking is, can we build neural networks that natively learn mappings between function spaces? That's the idea behind neural operators. The Fourier neural operator, for instance, learns in the frequency domain, which means it's resolution-independent. You can train at one resolution and evaluate at a much finer one, and it still respects the underlying physics in a way a standard CNN or transformer simply doesn't.

Why does that matter for foundation models? Because the bottleneck in physics isn't really the number of parameters, it's the cost of generating data. Every training example comes from either a very expensive simulation or a very expensive experiment. So a foundation model for physics has to be extremely data-efficient, and it has to generalize across geometries, boundary conditions, and even across different equations. We're already seeing early versions of this. In weather, neural operator models are now running tens of thousands of times faster than numerical weather prediction and matching or beating it on medium-range forecasts. We've used the same approach for carbon capture and storage, for plasma dynamics in fusion reactors, for designing medical catheters that reduce bacterial contamination. These were separate models, but the architecture is shared, and I think the next step is a single pretrained backbone that has absorbed a broad spectrum of physical phenomena and can be fine-tuned with very little data for a new domain.

The second piece is that these models have to be differentiable end to end, because the real prize isn't just prediction, it's design and control. If I can backpropagate through a surrogate of the physics, I can optimize the shape of an aircraft wing or the control signals in a tokamak directly. That turns science and engineering from a loop of simulate, inspect, tweak, repeat into something closer to gradient descent on the real world.

And the third piece, which I think people underestimate, is the interaction with language models. Large language models are very good at the symbolic layer — reading literature, proposing hypotheses, writing code. But they don't have a grounded model of physical reality. A physics foundation model gives them that grounding. You can imagine an agent that reasons in natural language about an experiment, calls a neural operator to simulate it in milliseconds, looks at the result, and iterates. That combination is what I think an AI scientist actually looks like.

What I'd caution against is thinking we can just scale the current paradigm and physics will fall out. Scale helps, but you need the right inductive biases. You need to respect conservation laws, symmetries, multi-scale structure. Otherwise you get models that look impressive on benchmarks and then violate basic physics the moment you push them out of distribution. So I see the future as a marriage: the scale and generality we've learned from language models, combined with the mathematical structure that physics gives us for free. If we get that right, I genuinely think we could compress decades of scientific discovery into years.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a single pretrained backbone that absorbs a broad spectrum of physical phenomena and can be fine-tuned for new domains.

r002.rationale: It proposes generalization across domains and equations, but does not say the models capture coupling among different physical processes.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is to move from models that learn patterns in language to models that learn how physical systems evolve. But that requires more than simply scaling up the same recipe. In physics, we care about conservation laws, stability, and whether a prediction remains reliable under conditions the model hasn’t seen before.

One promising direction is learning operators—the mappings between functions—so a model can work across different initial conditions, geometries, and resolutions. That could let us build a foundation model that we adapt to a new physical problem with relatively little additional data, instead of training a separate model for every simulation.

I also see these models working closely with numerical solvers and experiments. A fast model can help us explore a much larger design space, and then we can use higher-fidelity simulations or measurements to validate the most promising candidates. The exciting part is that this changes what we can ask: we can move from predicting how a particular design behaves to searching for designs that achieve a desired behavior.

The key challenge is knowing when to trust the model. Speed is valuable, but for scientific discovery and engineering, we also need accuracy, uncertainty estimates, and ways to recognize when we’re outside the model’s domain.

r001.rationale: The response discusses models that generalize across initial conditions, geometries, resolutions, and new physical problems, but does not clearly say they work across a broad range of physical phenomena.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe capturing interactions or coupling among different physical processes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is to build foundation models that learn the dynamics of the physical world, so we can adapt them to many different scientific and engineering problems without starting from scratch each time.

But physics poses some distinct challenges. You have to handle different geometries, boundary conditions, and scales. And a prediction that looks plausible is not enough—it needs to respect the underlying physics and be accurate enough for the decision you’re making.

That’s why I see a strong role for combining learning with numerical methods. Neural operators, for example, give us a way to learn mappings between functions, which is a natural language for physical systems. The goal is to bring together simulation, observational data, and physical constraints, while being able to quantify uncertainty.

What excites me most is closing the loop: using these models to explore designs, guide experiments, and discover better solutions. That could make scientific computing much more accessible and accelerate the pace at which we can test ideas.

r001.rationale: It proposes models that learn physical-world dynamics and adapt to many scientific and engineering problems, indicating use across a broad range of physical phenomena.

r002.rationale: It mentions different geometries, scales, numerical methods, data, and constraints, but does not say the models capture coupling among distinct physical processes.
